newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Australian inflation not credited - RBA.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Australian inflation not credited - RBA.

text.p: Australia's central bank believes that financial markets have not given sufficient credit to Australia's low inflation performance in the 1990s.

Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Governor Ian Macfarlane took the opportunity to raise this point when delivering a keynote address to the annual general meeting of the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) in Sydney on Thursday.
Macfarlane said Australia's low inflation performance this decade was not a "flash in the pan" and would continue.

"I think Australia has actually been slow to receive the recognition that it deserves for its monetary policy framework and for much its much better inflation record that now prevails," Macfarlane told the meeting.
Australian 10-year bonds were trading at a margin of more than 130 points over U.S. 10 year Treasuries on Thursday, having traded at a low of 75 points earlier this year.
After a 15 year period from 1974 to 1989 of high inflation, "Australia in the 1990s has clearly resumed it's place among the ranks of low inflation countries," Macfarlane said.
This low inflation environment, which had enhanced the economy's capacity for sustained long term growth, flowed from a evolution of the structure of monetary policy, he said.
The Reserve Bank of Australia targets the underlying inflation rate, aiming to keep it to an average of two to three percent over a run of years.
This target was introduced in 1993, and is supported by the government. As well, Macfarlane said the structure of monetary policy had beeen improved by increased RBA accountability and independence.

In the year to December, the underlying inflation rate was 2.1 percent, and on Thursday Macfarlane said the RBA's expectation was that it would continue at around that level for the foreseeable future.
In its quarterly report on the economy released last month, the RBA said it expected underlying inflation to be in the two to three percent range in 1998.
Macfarlane said that in the 1990s inflation had averaged 2.8 percent, compared with 3.8 percent amongst OECD countries.
"And our inflation over that period of seven years has been lower than such traditional low inflation countries such as Germany and Switzerland, not to mention the U.S.," he said.
One of the benefits of low inflation was its ability to enhance sustained economic growth, and Macfarlane said that the Australian economy was free of major macro economic imbalances.
The economy had experienced 5-1/2 years of uninterrupted economic growth, at an average of about 3.5 percent, which was higher than most other OECD countries, he said.

"Our economy remains free of major macro-economic imbalances at the moment and looking ahead we see we have a fair chance of achieving the sort of sustained growth that we achieved in the 1950s and the 1960s," Macfarlane said.
